title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: earthly king analogy fails — strength from crown's destination
pass_a_gloss: Lastly, as to the likeness brought of an earthly King destining a crown to those ascending the walls of a city: it has an immense unlikeness in that very point on which the whole force of the argument depends. For if no one could ascend by his own powers, and that King could inspire these powers into whomsoever he pleased, the crown would no longer have been destined to those to whom he would grant these powers from foresight of the ascent; but the foresight of the ascent and the inspired powers would be from the destination of the crown. And thus the matter stands most plainly between God and men.
pass_b_english: Last: the earthly-king crown analogy fails at the very hinge of the argument. If no one could climb by his own strength, and the king could breathe that strength into whomever he chose, the crown would not be destined from foresight of the climb — the climb foreseen, and the strength given, would flow from the crown's destination. That is exactly how it stands between God and men.
source_text: Postremo, quod attinet ad similitudinem allatam de Rege terreno coronam destinante adscendentibus muros civitatis; ingentem habet dissimilitudinem in illa ipsa re, unde tota vis argumenti dependet. Nam si nemo possit suis viribus adscendere, & Rex ille possit vires hasce quibus visum fuerit inspirare, non jam illis quibus hasce vires tribueret, destinata fuisset corona ex praevisione adscensionis; sed praevisa adscensio & vires inspiratae, ex destinatione coronae. At sic res habet planissime inter Deum & homines.
